questions.question: What triggers cache eviction?

options.text: Cache reaching capacity and needing space for new entries

questions.explanation: Eviction occurs when cache is full and new data needs to be stored. The eviction policy determines which existing entries to remove. TTL expiration is different from capacity-based eviction.

questions.question: What does LRU (Least Recently Used) eviction policy remove?

options.text: The oldest entry by creation time

questions.explanation: LRU evicts the entry that hasn't been accessed for the longest time, assuming recently accessed data is more likely to be accessed again. It tracks access time, not creation time.

questions.question: How does LFU (Least Frequently Used) differ from LRU?

options.text: LFU evicts based on access count; LRU evicts based on recency
LFU only works with distributed caches

questions.explanation: LFU tracks how often each entry is accessed and evicts the least frequently used. LRU tracks when entries were last accessed. LFU favors consistently popular items; LRU favors recently accessed items.

questions.question: A cache uses FIFO (First In, First Out) eviction. What is a potential problem?

options.text: It may evict frequently accessed items just because they were added early

questions.explanation: FIFO ignores access patterns—a heavily used item added early gets evicted before a rarely used item added later. LRU/LFU consider actual usage, making them generally more effective.

questions.question: Which eviction policy is best for a cache where some items are accessed in bursts but rarely otherwise?
questions.explanation: Pure LFU would keep burst items too long after the burst. Pure LRU might evict them during the burst. Hybrid policies like LRFU balance recency and frequency for varied access patterns.

questions.question: What is the 'cache pollution' problem?

options.text: Cache data becoming corrupted due to concurrent writes
Infrequently used items filling cache and evicting useful items
Cache entries exceeding their configured TTL values
Too many cache misses causing backend overload

questions.explanation: Cache pollution occurs when one-time or rarely-reused data fills the cache, evicting frequently accessed items. This reduces hit rate. Scan-resistant policies help prevent pollution.

questions.question: True or False: LRU is always the best eviction policy.
questions.explanation: LRU works well for many workloads but not all. Sequential scans can pollute LRU caches. LFU may be better for stable popularity patterns. The best policy depends on access patterns.

questions.question: A database query cache uses LRU. A batch job scans the entire table once. What happens?

options.text: The scan evicts frequently used queries, degrading cache effectiveness
Nothing, batch jobs don't affect cache

questions.explanation: The sequential scan accesses many rows once, making them 'recently used' and evicting actually-useful cached queries. This is the classic LRU scan problem. Scan-resistant policies address this.

questions.question: What is TTL-based eviction?

options.text: Evicting entries when cache is full
Evicting entries after a specified time period regardless of access

questions.explanation: TTL eviction removes entries after a set time, ensuring data freshness. It's independent of capacity-based eviction (LRU/LFU). Both can coexist—TTL for freshness, LRU for capacity.

questions.question: Which factors should influence eviction policy selection? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Access patterns determine LRU vs LFU effectiveness. Memory constraints affect how aggressively to evict. Freshness needs influence TTL settings. Programming language is irrelevant to eviction policy.

questions.question: What is 'random eviction' and when might it be appropriate?

options.text: Evicting entries randomly; appropriate when access is uniform
Evicting entries randomly; always the best choice
Evicting entries randomly; only for testing

questions.explanation: Random eviction is simple and has low overhead. When access patterns are uniform (no hot items), random performs similarly to LRU/LFU with less complexity. It's used in some CPU caches.

questions.question: A cache implements 'two-queue' or 'segmented LRU'. What problem does this solve?

options.text: Protecting frequently accessed items from being evicted by one-time accesses

questions.explanation: Segmented LRU uses multiple queues—new items enter a probationary queue and only move to protected queue on re-access. This prevents one-time scans from evicting valuable cached data.
